## What the model says

The signal discrimination model (SDM; [Oberauer, 2023](https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000328)) describes
errors in continuous reproduction with one distribution and no separate guessing parameter; the
model is available in the R package [bmm](https://venpopov.com/bmm/). Every
response error $x$ on the wheel has an activation that is highest at the target's colour and falls
with the distance from it in the shape of a von Mises distribution with the precision `kappa`; the
memory strength `c` scales it. The density is the exponential of the activation, divided by a
constant $Z$ that makes it integrate to 1. In bmm's default (`sqrtexp`) parametrization:

$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{Z} \exp\!\left( c \sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{2\pi}}\; e^{\kappa(\cos(x - \mu) - 1)} \right),
\qquad Z = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \exp\!\left( c \sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{2\pi}}\; e^{\kappa(\cos(x - \mu) - 1)} \right) dx
$$

In the equation $\mu$ is the location of the distribution, which bmm fixes at 0 unless `mu` is added
to the model formula in `bmf()`. The `bessel`
parametrization is the original one: the activation is
$c\, e^{\kappa \cos(x - \mu)} / (2\pi I_0(\kappa))$, with $I_0$ the modified Bessel function of order 0.
At `c` = 0 nothing is recalled and every error is equally likely, so guessing is not a separate
component but the limit of weak memory. With a larger `c` the density concentrates on the target;
`kappa` sets how narrow the concentration is.

## The task

One trial is a colour reproduction. The participant sees a display of coloured items, then one item
is cued, and the participant chooses its colour on a wheel. The response error is the angle between
the chosen colour and the target's colour on the wheel, in radians from −π to π. The SDM, in bmm,
uses a single signal, the target's colour, so that error is all it takes from the trial. The
colours of the other items, their locations and the set size are not inputs of the density, which is
why the Task settings panel is empty.

## Explore

The Predicted error distribution panel shows the density of the response error. Move `c` and the peak
rises while the distribution outside it sinks towards zero; move `kappa` and the peak changes its
width. The Activation and normaliser panel shows what the density is made of: the activation of each
error, whose height at 0° is set by `c` and whose width by `kappa`, and the constant $Z$ that turns
its exponential into a density. The readout under it gives $Z$, the density at the target and the
share of responses within ±20° of it, the window shaded in the density panel.

$Z$ has no closed form, and bmm computes it numerically too (with R's `integrate()`). This page sums
the exponential of the activation over 1024 equally spaced points of the circle, which matches
bmm's integral to better than 10⁻⁹ on the log density in every test of this site's code against bmm.

The `c` slider runs from 0 to 20 and the `kappa` slider from 0.1 to 50, moving evenly in log units for
`kappa`; the number fields show natural units. These ranges are this page's choice and do not come from the default priors,
which would give 0.78 to 70 for `c` and 0.61 to 55 for `kappa` (the prior mean ± 3 times the scale
0.75 on the log scale). The article names no ranges, and these cover every value it simulates and
fits. bmm estimates `c` on the log scale too, but its slider moves in natural units, because a
log scale has no place for `c` = 0, the limit at which every error is equally likely. bmm's default
priors are student_t(5, 2, 0.75) on log `c` and student_t(5, 1.75, 0.75) on log `kappa`; the starting
values, which the dashed curves keep, are their centres, $e^{2} = 7.39$ and $e^{1.75} = 5.75$. Typed
values outside the sliders' ranges are used as long as the density can be computed, and the hint under
the sliders says when a value lies beyond its slider. The radio buttons switch the parametrization.
The two give the same family of densities with different values of `c`, so switching converts `c`,
rounded to three digits in the number field, and the curve stays where it is. At `kappa` = 0 the
density is uniform for every `c` in both, so switching leaves `c` as it is. bmm converts with
`c_sqrtexp2bessel()` and `c_bessel2sqrtexp()`. Reset returns everything to the starting values.

## In bmm

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="sdm-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="sdm-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/sdm.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `dsdm()` returns the density of the response error in radians, in
the parametrization chosen above. `sdm()` defines the model for a data set in which each row is a
trial and `resp_error` holds the response error in radians; the model it fits uses the `sqrtexp`
parametrization, so under `bessel` the code also shows `c` converted. `bmf()` writes the formula
and `bmm()` estimates the parameters; `my_data` stands for your own data, and fitting runs Stan
through brms. See the [SDM article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_sdm_simple.html) and the
reference pages for [`sdm()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/sdm.html) and
[`dsdm()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/SDMdist.html). bmm cites the model as Oberauer, K.
(2023). Measurement models for visual working memory—A factorial model comparison.
*Psychological Review, 130*(3), 841-852. <https://doi.org/10.1037/rev0000328>
